title: # The Leadership, Thought, and Psychology of the Rebbe Rabbi Shmuel Bornsztain of Sochaczew – Author of the Shem MiShmuel

# Leadership, Thought, and Psychology of the Soul of the Admor Rabbi Shmuel Bornsztain of Sochatchov – Author of the *Shem MiShmuel*

The text surveys the multifaceted figure of Rabbi Shmuel Bornsztain of Sochatchov, author of the monumental work *Shem MiShmuel* ("A Name from Samuel"), through an analysis of his intellectual growth in the shadow of the Kotzk legacy and the methodology of his father, the *Avnei Nezer* ("Stones of the Crown"). The article presents the history of the Sochatchov Hasidic dynasty across generations, and emphasizes the transition from Polish leadership to renewed centrality in modern Israel. At the ideational center, the author analyzes the Admor's psychology of the soul and Hasidic psychology, which emphasizes the need for a harmonious connection between intellect and emotion and the nullification of the ego before divine truth. Finally, the text addresses the complex relationship of the *Shem MiShmuel* to the settlement of the Land of Israel, and explains how his writings became a central source of inspiration specifically among the religious-Zionist public, which sees in his teaching a bridge between spiritual holiness and practical life.

## Leadership, Thought, and Psychology of the Soul of the Admor Rabbi Shmuel Bornsztain of Sochatchov – Author of the *Shem MiShmuel*

### Introduction and Biographical Background: The Growth of a Prodigy in the Shadow of the *Avnei Nezer* and the Rebbe of Kotzk

Rabbi Shmuel Bornsztain of Sochatchov (4 Heshvan 5617, October 16, 1856 – 24 Tevet 5686, January 10, 1926), known by the name of his monumental composition as the author of the *Shem MiShmuel*, represents a unique meeting point and ideational peak in the world of Polish Hasidism at the end of the nineteenth century and the beginning of the twentieth century.[1] He was born in the town of Kotzk to his father Rabbi Avraham Bornsztain, founder of Sochatchov Hasidism and author of the responsa literature *Avnei Nezer* and the halakhic work *Eglei Tal* ("Dew Drops").[1, 2, 3, 4] Through his father, who was the distinguished son-in-law of Rabbi Menahem Mendel Morgenstern – "the Seraph" of Kotzk, the *Shem MiShmuel* was the direct grandson of the founder of the Kotzk approach, and even merited in his early childhood to dwell in the shadow of his great grandfather during the first three years of his life.[1, 2, 3]

Rabbi Shmuel's childhood period was characterized by frequent relocations and severe material poverty.[1] At age eight his family moved to the town of Przchów, where the deprivation in their home was so deep that he was often forced to walk to his studies without a piece of bread.[1] Despite the complex physical conditions, and being an only son to his parents alongside a single sister, his father the *Avnei Nezer* concentrated the majority of his educational efforts and spiritual investment in him.[3] This investment bore rapid fruit, and Rabbi Shmuel grew into an immense Torah scholar both in nigleh (revealed Torah) and nistar (esoteric Torah).[2, 3]

In his youth, Rabbi Shmuel engaged in trade in wine and various goods for his livelihood, and in parallel served as his father's right hand in disseminating Torah in the first Hasidic yeshiva that the *Avnei Nezer* established in Krushnovitz.[3] His most significant role in those days was editing his father's writings; he arranged and edited "the internal abbreviated section" of the famous halakhic work *Eglei Tal* on the laws of Shabbat, while his father wrote the lengthy commentary surrounding it.[1, 3] This deep involvement in his father's casuistic and analytical method of study shaped his intellectual style, which combines sharp halakhic scholarship, kabbalistic philosophy, and practical Hasidic thought.[2, 3]

### The Sochatchov Dynasty: Leadership Continuity and Generational Transition

Sochatchov Hasidism was always characterized by a combination of sharp scholarly learning, accepted in the Lithuanian yeshiva world, together with the existential storm of Kotzk.[2, 3] In order to understand the historical positioning of the *Shem MiShmuel* and the long-term influence of the dynasty, a comprehensive comparative table of the Hasidic admors across generations is presented below:

The examination of the leadership sequence reveals how the Sochatchov dynasty, which was almost completely destroyed in Europe, succeeded in rising from the dust in the Land of Israel.[3] The current Admor, Rabbi Shmuel Yitzchak Bornsztain, created through his children's marriages an extensive network of family connections with the leadership of the Hasidic world in the Land.[6] These alliances with the Stryków, Biała, and Boyan courts illustrate the dynasty's renewed centrality within the modern Haredi and Hasidic public, and ensure the continuity of the scholarly and intellectual legacy of the court's founders.[6]

### The Transition to Leadership and the Writing of the Composition *Shem MiShmuel*

With the passing of his father the *Avnei Nezer* in the year 5670 (1910), the yoke of leadership was placed on the shoulders of Rabbi Shmuel, who was then about 56.[3] Initially he firmly refused to accept the position of Admor upon himself out of deep fear lest leadership of the public lead to the nullification of his private Torah study, but the heavy pressure of the elder Hasidim convinced him.[3] He moved his residence to the city of Zgerz and afterwards to Otwock, stood at the head of a large yeshiva that attracted many exceptional scholars from Poland, and in parallel continued to engage in copying, editing, and publishing hundreds of his father's halakhic responsa, which appeared in the *Avnei Nezer* responsa series.[1, 3]

During approximately fifteen years of his leadership, Rabbi Shmuel delivered every Shabbat and holiday deep and complex homilies before his Hasidim.[1, 3] These homilies combined kabbalistic and philosophical theories with profound psychological analysis of the human soul.[3] Rabbi Shmuel would commit his Torah teaching to writing immediately after Shabbat or the holiday, but chose not to print them during his lifetime; he recorded the material in extreme brevity and in outline form out of concern that the general public would not penetrate to the depth of his profound and original thought.[3]

Only after his passing in the year 5686 (1926), did his son and successor, Rabbi David Bornsztain (author of the *Hasidei David*), take the manuscripts, decipher them, and begin to publish them.[2, 3] The printing of the book continued for several years and encompassed eight volumes in its first edition.[1] The book was called *Shem MiShmuel*, a name based on a wordplay from the Mishnah in tractate Shabbat: "Rabbi said: We find a small name from a great name, 'Shem' from Shimon and Shmuel...".[3] The composition incorporates Torah teachings he heard from his father the *Avnei Nezer* and also brings material from his grandfather the Rebbe of Kotzk, and it constitutes living testimony to the continuity of the spiritual dynasty.[2, 3]

### His Torah System and Thought: In-Depth Analysis of His Ideational Foundations

The teaching of the *Shem MiShmuel* rests on a dynamic conception of the human soul and of divine providence in the world, while translating abstract kabbalistic concepts into practical psychological terms.[3, 8] Rabbi Shmuel does not content himself with classical textual interpretation, but always strives to expose the forces operating behind the scenes of the biblical narrative and the halakhic dispute.[3, 8]

### Unity of Mind and Heart: The Dispute Between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on the Fifteenth of Shevat

A prominent example illustrating the *Shem MiShmuel*'s intellectual method is his famous analysis of the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the date of the New Year for trees.[3] Beit Shammai determines that the New Year for trees falls on the first of Shevat, while Beit Hillel determines that it falls on the fifteenth of that month.[3]

Rabbi Shmuel removes this halakhic dispute from its narrow botanical domain and connects it to two principled ways in God's governance of the world and in the human soul [3]:

**The approach of Beit Shammai (the first of Shevat):** represents the world of potential and raw power (the aspect of "mind").[3] On the first of Shevat the sap rises in the trees from within, even though outwardly the tree still appears dry and bare.[3] The mind, representing abstract intellect, is capable of recognizing this internal truth even without external expression.[3]

**The approach of Beit Hillel (the fifteenth of Shevat):** represents the world of deed and actual realization (the aspect of "heart").[3] On the fifteenth of Shevat, a day of the moon's fullness, the internal potential begins to be revealed outwardly in the form of buds and fruits.[3] The heart and emotion need to see the practical realization in order to be aroused.[3]

From this analysis, the *Shem MiShmuel* derives practical guidance in divine service, dealing with the place of mind and heart in spiritual life.[3] He explains that human perfection is achieved only when there exists a harmonious flow between the two: the mind must absorb the internal and abstract spiritual truth (Beit Shammai), but it is obligated to bring it into the heart and actual deed so that it may be revealed in the physical world (Beit Hillel).[3]

### Breaking the Shell of the Ego:
# The Secret of the Sign of the Serpent and the Descent into Egypt

An additional psychological depth is revealed in the commentary of the Shem Mishmuel on parashat Va'era, where he discusses the "sign of the serpent" that was presented before Pharaoh.[8] He raises a sharp difficulty: why did Moses perform three signs before the Children of Israel (serpent, leprosy, and blood), while before Pharaoh he sufficed with one sign alone—the transformation of the staff into a tanin, which is essentially a serpent? Ostensibly, it should have been the opposite, for the Children of Israel are "believers the children of believers," whereas Pharaoh the heretic required more numerous and convincing signs.[8]

Rabbi Shmuel's answer exposes his conception regarding the structure of evil and the kelipah in the human soul [8]:

The Kelipah of Egypt and Pharaoh: Pharaoh represents the pinnacle of pride and egoism, as the prophet describes him: "My river is my own, and I have made myself."[8] This kelipah does not stem from lack of information or intellectual doubts that can be resolved through numerous signs, but from an inflated self-"existence" and a boundless ego.[8] The tanin (or great water serpent) is the kabbalistic symbol of the cosmic ego and absolute pride.[8]

The Mechanism of Breaking: To contend with Pharaoh's kelipah of pride, there was no point in complex signs intended to convince the intellect.[8] The only way to subdue the inflated ego was to present before him the root of his existence—the tanin—and to show how Moses's staff swallows the staffs of the Egyptian magicians.[8] The swallowing of the staffs made clear to Pharaoh that his entire ostensibly independent existence is nothing but an illusion, and that his vital energy is derived from and completely nullified before the divine source.[8]

From this the Shem Mishmuel derives a fundamental psychological principle of avodah: to defeat the evil inclination and break the kelipah that prevents a person from advancing spiritually, one must not enter into intellectual negotiation with it or attempt to fight its many details.[8] The correct way is uprooting the root of evil, found in the pride and self-existence of the person, through the quality of bitul and absolute devotion to divine truth.[8]

# The Nature of Beauty and Aesthetics in Scripture

The Shem Mishmuel also devotes attention to the analysis of aesthetic concepts in Scripture, such as the descriptions of the beauty of biblical figures.[2] Scripture explicitly mentions the beauty of several of the patriarchs and matriarchs: of Rachel it is said "and Rachel was beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance"; of Joseph it is written "and Joseph was beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance"; and of Queen Esther it is said "and the maiden was beautiful of form and good of appearance."[2]

Rabbi Shmuel analyzes the difference between "beautiful of form" and "beautiful of appearance" or "good of appearance" as a deep psychological and spiritual distinction [2]:

Beautiful of form: Refers to external physical beauty, to the geometric proportions of the body and face.[2] This is a complete and perfected material vessel.[2]

Beautiful/Good of appearance: Refers to the spiritual projection, to the inner light and soul-vitality that shines through the eyes and face.[2] This is the content that fills the external vessel.[2]

The combination of the two in the figures of Rachel, Joseph, and Esther teaches that biblical beauty is not merely a superficial bodily trait, but rather evidence of an absolute harmony in which the external bodily vessel (to'ar) is perfectly matched to and projects the inner soul-light (mar'eh).[2]

# The Lamps of Aaron and the Eternal Light

Another significant matter in the thought of the Shem Mishmuel is the analysis of the role of Aaron the Priest in lighting the Menorah, a topic that received expansion and praise from the subsequent Rebbes of the dynasty.[2] Rabbi Shmuel explains that Aaron's lamps do not illuminate only the physical space of the Temple, but constitute a symbol of the kindling of the souls of all Israel.[2] The role of the tzaddik and leader of the generation is to identify the divine spark hidden in every person, even one who is at the lowest level, and to awaken it until the light rises on its own and becomes an independent flame that illuminates the entire world.[2]

# Divine Service in Practice: The Theory of "Internalization" and the Joy of Torah

The practical teaching of the Shem Mishmuel is based on the uncompromising demand for truth he inherited from his grandfather of Kotzk, according to which one must not be satisfied with external and mechanical fulfillment of commandments, but must aspire to the penetration of truth into the psychic structure of the person.[2]

## The Theory of "Internalization"

In Kotzk the expression "learn to internalize within yourself" was current.[2] The Shem Mishmuel developed this principle and made it a cornerstone of his educational and spiritual system.[2] True learning is not measured by the quantity of knowledge accumulated, but by the degree of influence of that knowledge on the character, qualities, and behavior of the learner.[2] When a Hasid told the Rebbe of Kotzk that he had finished studying all of Shas, the Rebbe asked him the key question: "But what has Shas taught you?" [2] Internalization is the existential understanding that the learner does not remain an observer from the side, but is fundamentally transformed as a result of the encounter with Torah.[2]

## Pleasure and Joy in Study as Service "for Its Own Sake"

Another central aspect of the Sochatchov system, which received comprehensive foundation from the Avnei Nezer and the Shem Mishmuel, deals with the relationship between joy and pleasure and Torah study.[2] Rabbi Shmuel opposed the common error among some people, who thought that Torah study is considered "for its own sake" only when the learner suffers, toils, and feels no personal enjoyment from the study.[2]

The Avnei Nezer and the Shem Mishmuel clarified that this approach is completely mistaken and contrary to the nature of the soul.[2] The Avnei Nezer wrote explicitly that one who studies and innovates novellae, and rejoices and delights in his study—this is the essence of study for its own sake.[2] Relying on the words of the holy Zohar, the Shem Mishmuel explained that the good inclination and the evil inclination both grow from joy; in the place where pleasure and joy stem from Torah study, there the good inclination grows and the person becomes attached to Torah with every fiber of his soul.[2] Joy and intellectual pleasure are not a disturbing factor, but are themselves the spiritual fuel that enables the soul to connect to Torah with an existential and deep connection.[2]

# The Land of Israel, Rectification of the Sin of the Spies, and the Tension vis-à-vis Zionism

Love of the Land of Israel and deep yearning for it were deeply rooted in the Bornstein family.[3] Already the father of the Shem Mishmuel, author of the Avnei Nezer, ruled in his responsa that there is a great commandment to endeavor with the various governments to ascend to the Land of Israel, and that the purchase of a holding in the Land is considered settlement of the Land even for one who actually resides in the Diaspora.[3] This theoretical love was translated into practice in the year 5651 (1891), when the Avnei Nezer sent his son, the Shem Mishmuel, to visit the Land of Israel and to purchase lands in it for settlement by the Hasidim of Sochatchov.[3] Although the practical mission failed due to the prohibition of the Ottoman authorities on foreign subjects purchasing lands, it left a deep imprint on the thought of Rabbi Shmuel.[3]

## The Theological Explanation for the Sin of the Spies

In his book, the Shem Mishmuel devotes many passages to the virtue of the Land and the secret of settlement in it.[3] In his famous discourse on parashat Shelach (5673), he proposes an original psychological-theological analysis of the sin of the spies.[3] He asks: how could people who were "princes of the congregation," "heads of the Children of Israel," despise the desirable Land and refuse to enter it? [3]

Rabbi Shmuel's explanation sheds new light on the portion [3]:

Life in the wilderness: The lives of the Children of Israel in the wilderness were completely spiritual and supernatural.[3] The manna descended from heaven, water flowed from the well, and the clouds of glory protected them.[3] In this reality they were exempt from any burden of livelihood and material life, and could occupy themselves solely with Torah study and detached spiritual elevation.[3]

Life in the Land of Israel: With entry into the Land, the divine governance was to change to natural governance.[3] The people were required to engage in wars, to plow, sow, reap, and maintain a complete economic and political system.[3]

The spies, according to the Shem Mishmuel, did not sin out of a desire to rebel against God, but out of "excessive" and misguided spirituality.[3] They preferred to remain in the wilderness in order to continue to delight in spiritual and pure Torah study, and feared that engagement with material life and action in the Land of Israel would lead to their spiritual decline.[3]

Rabbi Shmuel states categorically that this is a grave error.[3] The desir
The supreme divine ideal is not that man isolate himself in spiritual heights, but rather that he enter into the life of deed and matter and sanctify them.[3] The essence of the Divine Presence and the supreme necessity are realized specifically in the Land of Israel, a place where holiness is revealed through plowing, sowing, and contending with the challenges of physical reality.[3]

His Opposition to Political Zionism

Despite his immense yearning for the Land of Israel and his elevation of the value of labor and settlement there to the highest theological rank, the "Shem MiShmuel" vigorously opposed the modern Zionist movement as well as the "Mizrachi" movement (religious Zionism).[3] This opposition stemmed from two central factors[3]:

Reservations about cooperation with secular Jews: The concern that political and practical partnership with elements who do not observe Torah and mitzvot would lead to blurring of spiritual boundaries and damage to the religious character of the people.[3]

Messianic anxieties: The concern about establishing a political entity and sovereign rule before the coming of the Messiah and in a manner not guided by the full laws of the Torah.[3]

His Public Activity, His Influence on Agudat Yisrael, and His Family's Fate

Alongside his intellectual and scholarly work, the "Shem MiShmuel" was an active public leader in Poland before and during World War I.[1, 3] He was deeply involved in establishing Torah institutions and organizing Orthodox Jewish life in the state.[3, 9]

The Connection to Agudat Yisrael in Poland

The Sochatchov Hasidic movement was intimately involved in the establishment and activities of Agudat Yisrael in Poland.[9] One of the most prominent and influential hasidim of the Sochatchov court was Rabbi Alexander Zusya Friedman, author of the popular book "Ma'ayana shel Torah".[9] Rabbi Alexander Zusya served as general secretary of Agudat Yisrael in Poland and was among the architects of the educational and political path of Polish Orthodoxy.[9] He drew extensively from the Torah of the Sochatchov rebbes, and the dissemination of the "Shem MiShmuel's" ideas among the Jewish masses in Poland was accomplished largely through these channels.[9]

His Family's Fate and Its Branches

Rabbi Shmuel Bornsztain left behind an extensive family.[1, 3] He had 19 children from two wives, but most of them were murdered in the Holocaust along with the masses of Sochatchov hasidim in Poland.[3] Among his prominent sons were[1, 3]:

Rabbi David Bornsztain (the "Hasdei David"): His firstborn son and successor in the rebbedom.[1, 2, 3] He led the hasidut with a high hand in Poland between the world wars and was murdered in the Warsaw Ghetto in 5703 [1943].[3]

Rabbi Hanoch Henikh Bornsztain: Survived the Holocaust, immigrated to the Land of Israel, and reestablished the hasidic court in the Beit Vagan neighborhood of Jerusalem.[2, 3] He served as the first editor of the periodical "HaHed" and as chairman of the haredi division of the Jewish National Fund.[3]

Moshe Eliezer Bornsztain: Son of the "Shem MiShmuel" who chose a unique path and worked as a writer and playwright, indicating the wide variety and multifaceted talents that existed in this family.[1, 9]

Rabbi Aharon Yisrael Bornsztain: Among the rebbe's additional sons.[1]

The Modern Revival and Reception in Religious Zionism and Scholarship

One of the most fascinating processes in the history of the reception of hasidic literature in recent generations is the transformation of the book "Shem MiShmuel" into a prized asset specifically among the religious-Zionist public in the Land of Israel.[1, 3] Despite the author's original opposition to political Zionism, his thought grew deep bridges to the Zionist Torah world.[3]

The Historical Rectification by His Grandson in the War of Independence

The most dramatic expression of the closing of the circle between the Torah of the "Shem MiShmuel" and the Zionist enterprise is embodied in the figure of his grandson, Shmuel Avraham Bornsztain.[3] Shmuel Avraham was born in Poland on the 4th of Adar 5688 [1928], about two years after his great-grandfather's passing, and was named after his grandfather (Shmuel) and great-great-grandfather (Avraham, the "Avnei Nezer").[3] At age six he immigrated with his parents to Tel Aviv and grew up there.[3] At age 14 he joined the Gadna and the Haganah, and in the War of Independence he participated in defending the reapers in the fields of Tel Adashim in the Jezreel Valley.[3] On Lag BaOmer 5708 [1948], only two weeks after the Declaration of the State, he fell in battle and was brought to eternal rest in the military cemetery at Nahalat Yitzhak.[3]

Educators and thinkers in the religious-Zionist public point to the fall of Shmuel Avraham as a historical and practical rectification of the sin of the spies that his grandfather the "Shem MiShmuel" had discussed.[3] Whereas the spies rejected the Land and refused to engage in physical labor and warfare, the rebbe's grandson fought and fell for the revival of the people of Israel in its land, out of complete integration between the holiness of Torah and the defense of the plow and the Land.[3]

Rabbi Shabbetai Rappaport and the Scholarly Connection

Sarah Tzina, daughter of the "Shem MiShmuel," married Rabbi Shaul Rappaport.[3] Their son, the rebbe's grandson, is Rabbi Shabbetai Rappaport, who represents a central Torah and halakhic figure in contemporary religious Zionism.[3] Rabbi Rappaport served as a rosh metivta at Yeshivat Har Etzion, as head of Yeshivat Hesder "Shavut Yisrael" in Efrat, and as head of the Advanced Institute for Torah at Bar-Ilan University.[3] He is connected with every fiber of his being to his ancestors' legacy and teaches and disseminates his grandfather's Torah and halakha at every opportunity, while methodologically integrating sharp Sochatchov talmudism with scientific research and modern thought.[3]

Accessibility Projects: "LeOr HaShem" and "Mo'adei HaShem"

The immense popularity of the book "Shem MiShmuel" led to the development of leading accessibility initiatives.[3] Rabbi Eli Scheinfeld, a rosh metivta at Yeshivat Horev, published the books "LeOr HaShem" (spiritual notes and explanations on the weekly Torah portions) and "Mo'adei HaShem" (a contemporary and structured adaptation of the rebbe's Torah on the festivals).[3, 10]

Rabbi Scheinfeld describes how he discovered the book in his youth at Yeshivat HaGolan, and felt that only when he studied the words of the "Shem MiShmuel" did he find what his soul sought in understanding the essence of the festivals, and especially in the wondrous analysis linking the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the 15th of Shevat with the place of the mind and heart in the service of God.[3] Rabbi Shmuel's concentrated and profound writing invites the student to continue deepening and drawing from it lights that illuminate modern life here and now.[3]

Alongside this, comprehensive scholarly and talmudic works have been written analyzing the rebbe's intellectual system, including the series of books by the jurist and scholar Dr. Avi Weinrot, such as the book "LeOr Shem MiShmuel," which has received great appreciation and blessings from great Torah scholars and rebbes of our generation for the way it makes accessible and analyzes the foundations of Kotzk and Sochatchov thought.[2]

Summary

The rebbe Rabbi Shmuel Bornsztain of Sochatchov succeeded in creating a comprehensive theological and psychological thought system, constituting one of the most fascinating syntheses between the world of sharp talmudism and the profound Torah of hasidut.[2, 3] Through the use of analytical and structural tools, the author of the "Shem MiShmuel" succeeded in translating the storm of truth of Kotzk and the halakhic genius of Sochatchov into a language of the soul's powers, relevant to the modern student no less than to the hasidim in Poland of the early twentieth century.[2, 3]

The historical development of Sochatchov hasidut and its wide reception in the religious-Zionist public attest to the inexhaustible vitality of his thought.[3] Despite the author's original opposition to the political frameworks of Zionism, his Torah on the virtue of the Land of Israel, the obligation to integrate spirit and matter, and the necessary rectification of the sin of the spies has become a cornerstone in the edifice of the spiritual world of religious Zionism.[3] The continuity of the dynasty on the one hand, and his talmudic and intellectual influence on the other, ensure that the name and Torah of the "Shem MiShmuel" will continue to illuminate and shape the face of the Torah world and Jewish thought for many generations to come.[3, 6]

title: From Transgression to Merit: Transformation of Failures into Organizational Assets in the Teaching of the "Shem MiShmuel"

From Willful Sin to Merit: Transformation of Failures into Organizational Assets in the Doctrine of the Shem miShmu'el

1. Introduction: The Restorative Model of Sochatchov Hasidism

In an era of constant volatility and disruptions, modern leadership requires a capacity that extends beyond standard crisis management. While traditional approaches content themselves with "repair" (Repair)—restoring the system to the pre-crisis status quo—the philosophy of Rabbi Shmuel Bornsztain (the Shem miShmu'el) proposes a paradigm of restorative transformation.

The Sochatchov strategy is not merely theoretical; it emerged from extraordinary personal resilience. The Shem miShmu'el, who experienced the loss of most of his 21 children, formulated a leadership that does not ignore pain or failure, but rather uses them as raw material for reconstruction. Combining the analytical precision of his father (the Avnei Nezer) with the uncompromising sharpness of his grandfather (the Kotzker Rebbe), he offers managers a model in which failure is not an anomaly, but an accelerator for growth. The key lies in teshuvah me-ahavah (repentance from love)—a methodology of recalibration that transforms systemic "falls" into powerful engines of commitment.

2. The Recalibration Model: Transforming "Willful Sins" (Strategic Failures) into Merits

In the managerial mechanics of the Shem miShmu'el, failure (the "willful sin") is not merely an operational error, but potential for creating new kinetic energy. When an organization experiences distancing from its goals or its values—whether due to human error or a deliberate strategic gamble that failed—a "vacuum" is created that generates thirst and desire to return to the center.

Hasidism defines this as working be-ḥila yatir (with extra force): precisely the distance from the goal produces a striving intensity higher than that which existed in a state of linear success.

Stages of Strategic Transformation (from "Willful Sin" to "Merit"):

Identifying the Loss (Gap Analysis): Systemic recognition of the severity of the distance created from the organizational vision.

Bitterness of Soul (Organizational Accountability): Creating an internal shock that does not permit reconciliation with the existing situation, in contrast to the apathy of "material fatigue."

Intensifying the Thirst (Kinetic Desire): Converting the sensation of failure into an active drive for radical change.

Restorative Calibration (Transformation): Return to the organizational core from a desire in which the failure becomes the direct cause of the new strength.

The Managerial So What: A skilled leader uses severe crises to propel the organization to a level of adherence to the mission that could not have been achieved through ordinary means. The crisis becomes an asset the moment it redefines the boundaries of organizational will.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

3. The "Looking Down" Strategy: Transforming "Anger" into "Mercy" Through Investment in the Periphery

In crisis situations, the automatic dynamic of leadership is midat ha-din (the attribute of judgment)—searching for culprits, punishment, and intensifying tension. The Shem miShmu'el warns that hashkafah (looking from above downward) symbolizes in Scripture almost always "anger" and judgment. The sole case in which looking down becomes a blessing ("Look down from Your holy habitation... and bless") is in the context of "gifts to the poor."

In managerial terms: The ability to transform lethal systemic criticism (judgment) into an opportunity for rehabilitation (mercy) depends on the leader's focus. Only when the leader chooses to invest in the weakened links of the organization (in the organizational periphery, in weakened departments, or in employees who have been harmed) does he succeed in "sweetening" the judgment and transforming the crisis into a source of abundance.

4. The Psychology of Failure: "Mental Laziness" as the Root of Impulsive Haste

Analysis of the sin of the Golden Calf in the doctrine of the Shem miShmu'el reveals a deep cognitive failure: the "haste" ("they have been quick to turn aside from the way"). Contrary to the perception that speed is always an advantage, here it is presented as a symptom of "mental laziness."

The Shem miShmu'el (in the name of his grandfather of Kotzk) distinguishes between "lazy" and "deliberate":

The Lazy Person: Not one who does not act, but rather one who is too lazy to exercise judgment. He acts with impulsive speed in order to escape from the intellectual labor required for composure. The speed is a dangerous "shortcut" attempting to circumvent complex reality.

The Deliberate Person: A leader who exercises metinūt (deliberateness)—active work of refining intellect and heart under pressure. Deliberateness is a risk management tool that prevents organizational "Golden Calf sins" arising from imaginary time pressure.

The Managerial So What: Effective leadership requires delay of gratification and composure. Speed without deliberateness is not efficiency, but avoidance of genuine managerial work.

5. Embracing Leadership: Creating "Encompassing Lights" as a Resilience Wall

The leader's role is not only to manage tasks, but to create a "protective envelope" (or makif—encompassing light) that provides psychological security. In a foundational story, it is recounted how the Shem miShmu'el embraced a deceased person who sought correction (rectification of the past) and immediately afterward embraced a living hasid under stress (protection in the present), while declaring: "As long as you are with me—you have nothing to fear."

Leadership requires "strategic duality":

"Dove" Inward: Cultivating a culture of listening, submission, and growth.

"Beast" Outward: Powerful and aggressive defense against competitors and destructive external forces (mal'akhei ḥavalah—angels of destruction).

The "leadership embrace" creates an array of seven protective canopies (corresponding to the seven canopies surrounding Zion), enabling the organization's people to recover even from the "ghosts" of past failures. A strong leader protects the organization's inner point from the external kelipah (husk) attempting to penetrate inward at moments of weakness.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

6. Summary: Leadership as "Processing the Parchment" for the Organization

The leader is not a technical function, but "the heart of the entire congregation of Israel." The transformation of failure into an asset passes through the leadership heart, which unites the collective into a single entity.

Three Practical Recommendations for Restorative Leadership:

Heart Processing (Ibudah de-Klaf—Processing of the Parchment): Like the processing of leather before writing a Torah scroll, the leader must labor at refining his own motives and the organizational culture before launching a new strategy. Without "processing" the heart and culture, values will not be inscribed upon the tablet of the organization's heart.

Adopt "Restorative Looking Down": At a moment of crisis, shift the gaze from searching for culprits to active investment in rehabilitating the weakened parts of the system.

Operational Deliberateness: Beware of mental shortcuts. Develop resilience that permits waiting for full composure even when the market pushes toward impulsive action.

Genuine growth does not occur despite failures, but because of them. When a leader acts in the spirit of teshuvah me-ahavah, he builds a new, stronger, and more resilient organization, in which every "willful sin" of the past becomes a strategic "merit" ensuring the future.

1. Introduction: The Strategy of "Orot Makifim" (Encompassing Lights) (Strategic Buffering)

The Sochatchov methodology, as formulated by the Admor of Kotzk and refined by the "Shem MiShmuel," identifies the concept of "makifim" (encompassing lights) as a critical component in preserving organizational homeostasis and systemic security. In contrast to "inner lights" representing the system's current operational capacity, the "makifim" constitute a values-based and visionary envelope exceeding the boundaries of the existing "vessel."

The "makifim" strategy dictates a core principle: foundational institutional values (the makifim) must always exceed operational capacity (the inner lights). This surplus is not waste, but rather a "safety margin" protecting the inner point – the core vitality of the organization – from "external forces" (external pressures, crises, or cultural erosion). Without a positive external envelope, the organization is pushed to create a negative envelope (kelipah), sealing off the flow of information and vitality within it.

Body as Envelope (Refined Buffer): The leader's presence becomes a "fortified wall." Personal refinement ("processing of the parchment") transforms the leader's presence into something eternal and spiritual, constituting a physical and psychological barrier against threats.

Just as the Avnei Nezer identified negative potential (a child destined to become a priest) and the Shem miShmuel converted this into a "disguise" that enabled his survival in the Shoah, the strategic leader does not merely block threats but "dresses" the organization in an identity that exploits the threat's energy for survival (Organizational Camouflage).

4. Resilience Sequence: Consolidated Identity (Planting) as Prerequisite for Self-Criticism (Sowing)

The methodology establishes a rigid logical sequence in building resilience. In contrast to approaches that preach humility as a starting point, Sokatchov mandates graduated construction:

Stage A: Planting (Identity Construction): Instilling unit pride and assertiveness ("If I am not for myself, who is for me?"). The organization must first develop a "backbone" and powerful self-identity. Without recognition of self-worth ("and his heart was elevated in the ways of the Lord"), the organization will suffer "a fall from its level" and be vulnerable to contempt and external penetration.

Stage B: Sowing (Strategic Humility): Only after consolidation of identity can humility and self-nullification be implemented ("And when I am for myself, what am I?"). The controlled decay of the seed in the earth is a condition for growth, but is possible only for an entity possessing rooted vital force.

Strategic Insight: An organization lacking identity (without planting) cannot practice learning and humility (sowing); it will simply disintegrate. Resilience derives from the combination of the "lion" (assertiveness toward the outside) and the "dove" (obedience to core values).

The Centrality of the Teachings of Rabbi Shmuel Bornsztain

The "Shem miShmuel"

Executive Summary

This document summarizes the life history, thought, and influence of Rabbi Shmuel Bornsztain of Sokatchov (5616-5686, 1856-1926), the second Rebbe in the Sokatchover dynasty, who became known primarily through his foundational book "Shem miShmuel." Rabbi Shmuel, son of the author of the "Avnei Nezer" and grandson of the Kotzker Rebbe, poured into his writings a unique blend of brilliant scholarship, Hasidic depth, and penetrating psychological analysis. His thought strives toward the point of internal truth of the person, examining the hidden motivations behind his actions, even those performed inadvertently.

His teaching emphasizes the constant dialectic between poles: the individual and the collective, humility and self-confidence, the natural and the miraculous. He presents complex educational models requiring a person first to develop a strong and uncompromising "I," and only afterward to know how to nullify himself within the collective. Another central idea is "the virtue of beginning," according to which beginnings in life—the beginning of the yoke of commandments, marriage, or even the beginning of each day—have decisive power in shaping the entire continuation of the path. His book "Shem miShmuel," based on his discourses, has become an invaluable asset in the Jewish bookshelf, studied and revered in diverse circles for its clarity, originality, and great depth.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. His Life History and Roots

Rabbi Shmuel Bornsztain was born on the fourth of Cheshvan 5616 (1856) in the town of Kotzk in Poland. He was the only son of Rabbi Avraham Bornsztain, founder of Sokatchover Hasidism and author of the "Avnei Nezer," and his mother, Sarah Tzinah, was the daughter of Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Kotzk. His dual lineage, both to the scholarly court of Sokatchov and to the truth-seeking court of Kotzk, shaped his spiritual path.

The Story of His Birth and Name: When he was born, his father asked the Kotzker Rebbe what to name him. The Rebbe replied that he should call him whatever name came to mind at the time of circumcision. At that moment, the verse "and she called his name Samuel" arose in his father's mind, and thus he was called. This name was linked to Hannah's prayer, "for from the Lord I requested him," an idea that would influence his teaching.

Initially, Rabbi Shmuel refused to earn his livelihood from Torah and opened a shop for the wine trade. Only after his father's passing in the year 5670 (1910), and following pressure from the Hasidim, was he crowned as his successor as Rebbe and as rosh yeshivah. He conducted his court with Kotzker assertiveness.

His life was marked by personal tragedy; he had 21 children, and all perished in the Shoah. Despite the catastrophe, it is related that he accepted the judgment with love.

Like his father, he was an enthusiastic supporter of settlement in the Land of Israel. In the year 5651 (1891) he even visited the Land at his father's command to purchase lands for settlement, but his plan was thwarted by the Ottoman authorities.

Rabbi Shmuel passed away on the twenty-fourth of Tevet 5686 (1926) and was buried beside his father in Sokatchov.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2. The Book "Shem miShmuel": Its Composition and Influence

His central work, "Shem miShmuel," is a collection of Hasidic discourses on the Torah and the festivals delivered by him between the years 1910-1926 and written down by him afterward. The volumes were printed in Poland after his passing by his sons, Rabbi David and Rabbi Chanoch Henoch Bornsztain.

The book uniquely combines the teachings of his father,
# Translation

the *Avnei Nezer*, and his grandfather, the Rebbe of Kotzk, together with his original and profound insights. He is characterized by clarity, depth, and linguistic beauty, and occupies a central place in the Hasidic bookshelf. The work enjoys wide circulation and is studied in regular classes among diverse audiences—Hasidic, Lithuanian, and religious-Zionist alike.

His greatness was recognized even during his lifetime. Rabbi Meir Simcha ha-Kohen of Dvinsk, author of the *Or Sameaḥ* (*Joyous Light*), expressed himself in a famous statement:

"The world recognized the *Avnei Nezer*... in *nigleh* and the *Shem mi-Shmuel* in *nistar*. But I tell you that he is greater in *nigleh* than in *nistar*... Do you know what is the most beautiful composition that the *Avnei Nezer* left behind? I will tell you: it is his son, the *Shem mi-Shmuel*. He is the wondrous creation that the blessed *Avnei Nezer* left behind."

## 3. Foundational Themes in His Thought

The thought of the *Shem mi-Shmuel* is multidimensional and addresses a wide range of topics, while constantly striving to expose the inner layers of the soul and of divine service.

### a. Sin and Punishment: Investigating Inner Motivations

The *Shem mi-Shmuel* analyzes the nature of sin not merely as an external act, but as an expression of deep internal processes.

* **The Sin of the Golden Calf—The Sin of Haste**: According to his approach, the essence of the sin was not in the actual making of the calf, but in the "haste" (*saru maher min ha-derekh*, "they turned aside quickly from the way"). The haste stemmed from a lack of *yishuv ha-da'at* (settledness of mind), a kind of laziness in deepening one's thought, which led to rash action. In other words, the external stumbling arose from an internal defect.

* **The Sin-Offering—The Inadvertent as Expression of Hidden Desire**: Even a sin committed inadvertently is not accidental. He argues that a person stumbles into transgression inadvertently only because in the secret of his heart he desired it. Therefore, the sin-offering, which atones for inadvertence, is offered specifically on the northern (*tzafon*) side of the altar, alluding to the "hidden" (*tzafun*) and concealed thoughts in a person's heart.

* **Confronting Desire**: He discusses the rabbinic dictum: "A person should not say 'I cannot eat pig meat,' but rather should say 'I can and I desire to, but my Father in Heaven has decreed upon me.'" He explains that a person of true faith, who has internalized God's word, transforms the divine commandment into part of his very being. The prohibition becomes a "fortified wall" that places the object of desire outside the realm of reality, similar to a peasant who does not covet the king's daughter. If a person continues to desire the forbidden thing, this is a sign that his faith remains external and has not penetrated the depths of his soul.

### b. Human Education: Between Humility and Self-Confidence

The *Shem mi-Shmuel* presents a complex educational model requiring balance between two opposing approaches:

* **"Sowing" versus "Planting"**: He compares two methods of education. "Sowing" corresponds to an approach demanding self-nullification and absolute humility (like the seed that rots in the ground before it sprouts). "Planting" corresponds to an approach emphasizing the development of self-worth, responsibility, and greatness ("planted" and strong).

* **"If I Am Not for Myself, Who Will Be for Me"**: Basing himself on Hillel's saying, he argues that the correct order is to begin with "If I am not for myself, who will be for me"—the "planting" stage in which the person develops a strong, vigorous personality with self-awareness. Only after establishing an uncompromising "I" can he move to the second stage, "And when I am for myself alone, what am I"—the "sowing" stage, in which he knows how to nullify himself appropriately within society, to learn from others, and to conduct himself with humility.

### c. The Individual and Unity: The Dialectic of Oneness

A central idea in his thought is the tension and synthesis between the particular and the collective.

* **The Students of Rabbi Akiva**: He asks how it is possible that the students of Rabbi Akiva, who taught "Love your neighbor as yourself—this is the great principle of the Torah," did not show respect to one another. His answer is surprising: they did not show respect to one another because the love and unity among them were so absolute that they saw themselves as a single body. Just as a limb in the body does not "honor" another limb, so they saw no need for mutual respect. Their sin was that the unity nullified and obscured the uniqueness of each individual, and therefore they died.

* **The Time of the Counting of the Omer**: The timing of their deaths is not coincidental. The month of Iyyar, whose zodiac sign is the ox, symbolizes the uniqueness and independent-mindedness of the individual. The month of Nisan, whose sign is the lamb, symbolizes the collective (all lambs have a similar voice). The month of Sivan, whose sign is the twins, represents the ideal synthesis: unity ("as one man with one heart") alongside recognition of the unique value of each individual ("had Israel been lacking even one person, the Divine Presence would not have been revealed"). The plague ceased on Lag ba-Omer, when the light of this balance began to shine in anticipation of the giving of the Torah.

* **The Single Body of the People of Israel**: Based on the teaching of the Maggid of Mezritsh, he argues that the people of Israel has a dual existence: natural (separate bodies) and miraculous (a single collective body). This miraculous reality of unity is the reason, for example, that sacrifices are offered in a single central place, because the entire nation is a single body.

### d. The Power of Beginning (The Merit of *Reshit*)

The *Shem mi-Shmuel* attributes decisive importance to beginnings, from a conception that they contain within them the potential of all that follows.

* **The Stubborn and Rebellious Son**: His judgment is determined "on account of his end" because his corruption occurs at the *reshit* (beginning) of his path as an adult (the first three months after reaching bar mitzvah age). Since the beginning is corrupted, it is clear that the end will be as well.

* **The Firstborn**: He takes a double portion in inheritance because he is *reshit ono* (the first of his father's strength), and he is perceived as the cause and root of the brothers who come after him.

* **The Lesson for Life**: This is a great teaching for a person to be careful about *reshit* at every stage: the beginning of accepting the yoke of commandments, the beginning of marriage, the beginning of the year, and even the beginning of each day, for diligence in morning commandments draws after it the entire day.

### e. The *Makifim*: Spiritual Forces and the Protection of the Tzaddik

A central kabbalistic conception in his thought is the doctrine of the *makifim*—spiritual forces that envelop a person.

* **Kelipot versus Encompassing Light**: The forces of evil are called *kelipah* (husk) because they envelop and conceal the inner point of holiness. Against them, one can create an *or makif* (encompassing light) of holiness that protects the person.

* **The Tzaddik's Embrace**: It is told of a Hasid from Bendin who was next in line to die in a plague that struck his group. He traveled to the *Shem mi-Shmuel*, who, instead of answering his question, stood up and embraced him with a fierce embrace. The *Shem mi-Shmuel* explained later that just as he had embraced the soul of a deceased person to protect it from the angels of destruction, so he embraced the Hasid. The physical embrace created a spiritual *makif* of holiness, for the body of the tzaddik becomes spiritual and can serve as a "fortified wall" protecting against external forces.
